steps.say: On the last page, we learned that a function is a small reusable block of code. Now let us see how a function is written, and what parameters and arguments are.
A parameter is a variable in the function definition. An argument is the value that we pass to the function when we call it. This is a very common board exam question.

Look at the power function in the book. It has a requires line, which says b must be zero or more. It has a returns line, which says the answer is a to the power of b. Then the definition uses let rec, name pow, and parameters a and b. If b is zero it gives 1. Otherwise it multiplies a with another call.

board.title: Function without data types

steps.say: Notice that we did not write any data type here. Some compilers can find the types by themselves. For other compilers, writing the type is compulsory. In this example, the if expression gives 1, so its type is int, and so the function returns int. Since b is compared with zero, b is int. Since a is multiplied, a is also int.

board.title: No data type given: compiler infers a, b and result as int

steps.say: Now the same function with data types. This is called type annotation. When we write type annotations, the brackets are a must. Writing types clearly helps us to understand error messages.

board.title: Function with data types

steps.say: Now the syntax. The word let introduces the definition. Then comes the function name, then the parameters, then the assignment symbol, and then the expression. For a function that calls itself, we use let rec instead of let. Such a function is called a recursive function. If it is not recursive, we can leave out rec.

board.title: Syntax of function definition
board.body: let rec fn a1 a2 ... an := k

steps.say: Here is the factorial example. If n is zero, it returns 1. Otherwise it multiplies n with factorial of n minus 1. Also remember, in a definition like a assigned 24, the value 24 is bound to the name a. A definition is not an expression.

board.title: Factorial
board.body:
(Requires: n>= 0)
let rec fact n :=
    if n = 0 then 1
    else
        n * fact(n-1)

steps.say: Finally, function types. x arrow y means one input of type x and output of type y. x1 arrow x2 arrow y means two inputs and one output. Also remember, all functions are static. There is no dynamic function definition. Well done, you are doing great!

board.title: x → y : one input type x, output type y
x1 → x2 → y : two inputs, output y

explainAgain.say: Think of a school canteen counter. The counter has a rule: you give a token and it gives you a snack. The empty space for the token in the rule is the parameter. Your actual token, say number 5, is the argument.

board.title: Parameter = empty slot in the rule

explainAgain.say: Now think of a recursive function like a student asking a friend in the next bench to solve a smaller sum. That friend asks the next one, and so on, until someone gets a very easy one, like zero. That easy case is the stopping point. Without it, the chain never ends.

board.title: Recursive = calls itself on a smaller problem, stops at base case

example.say: Let us trace factorial of 3. Factorial of 3 is 3 times factorial of 2. Factorial of 2 is 2 times factorial of 1. Factorial of 1 is 1 times factorial of 0. Factorial of 0 is 1, which stops the calls. Now multiply back: 1, then 1, then 2, then 6. Here n is the parameter and 3 is the argument.

checkQuestion.question: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument? Also, which keyword do we use to define a recursive function?
checkQuestion.idealAnswer: A parameter is a variable in the function definition. An argument is the value passed to the function when it is called. A recursive function, which calls itself, is defined using let rec.
